samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Edward T. Johnson was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of Mr. Edward Johnson, World War II Veteran Edward T. Johnson. Mr. Johnson served with the U.S. Army's Ninth Ordnance Battalion, Sixth and Eighth Armies. He served in the Pacific theater, and his highest rank was First Lieutenant, Ordnance. I'm Tom Swope, and we recorded this at Mr. Johnson's home in Painesville, Ohio, on September 28, 2001. Mr. Johnson's age at the time of this recording was 81.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Actually, we started for the war from the family farm house, which is right across the street. We were living upstairs, 969 Riverside Drive. That was my wife's parents' farmhouse, and we had a couple rooms and a kitchen upstairs.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news about Pearl Harbor?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Yes, I do. I was working at the old Standard Portland Cement Company, and I went to work that day from 3:00 to 11:00, 3:00 in the afternoon. And when -- I got to the check-in where we had to punch in our time cards, and they asked if I had the word, and I said, "Well, I heard something on the radio that the Japanese had bombed Pearl Harbor." I said, "Boy, I sure feel sorry for the Japanese," because I had just read an article in a national magazine that if the Japanese started anything we could go over there and in three months' time we would have their country leveled, we were far superior and they didn't know anything, and et cetera. Well, so I realized that I was tired of working at the cement plant. I had two years of chemical engineering in college, and I had three years of work in the heavy chemicals industry and I wanted out. So I took a job out. I went with the Cleveland Ordnance District as an inspector. They trained me. I went out on the job. Actually, I was stationed in Akron, and I used to come home weekends when I could. Our oldest son was born in July following Pearl Harbor. And incidentally, my wife and I were married in June of 1941, and our son was born in July of the next year. So there we were with a baby boy and a new job and war on our hands. So I enjoyed the work and it was very nice, but I also realized that I had to do a little more for the country and for my family; they were important to me, and so I went into the service. There was a special program that I heard about, volunteer officer candidate. You could volunteer for the military service, and if you finally made it into -- were accepted in officer candidate school and the actual program, you would get the training. And any time up until the time that you were commissioned -- in other words, if you washed out of the place or before then, you could ask for a discharge and get it. To be in the program, you had to have two years of college, you had to be a 3A classification, which is married men with children, and I fit. So I took the program and was sent to Aberdeen Proving Ground, because I had been in ordnance. And I went through basic training, technical training, cadre school, and I was accepted for officer candidate school. In the end of 1943, I was commissioned. So I did a couple more months of training at Aberdeen and went to the South Pacific. I got home --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When was that?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: I went over in first of May 1943 -- yeah. 1943.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: And that ordnance job was an army job? What was --

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: I worked for the Cleveland Ordnance District. And it was a civilian -- civil service, is what it was. And I was stationed at Akron. And Firestone Tire and Rubber Company was making a 40-millimeter Bofors antiaircraft cannon. That was my main job. But I also went to outside plants who were -- to subcontractors and checked the parts that they were sending in to us and other places. Very interesting job. I liked it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But in officer candidate school you weren't actually in the army?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You were in the army?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Yes. I enlisted in the army on the 1st of May.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: But you could have gotten out of it at any time?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Yes, I could have. I could have, yeah. Let me get my dates straight. I enlisted the 1st of May of '43. I wanted to wait until our son was about a year old or so before -- make sure my wife was safe with the boy and everything, and then I'd go. And I was commissioned on the 31st of December of '43. So I went overseas in May of '44 and I came back in May of '46. So I guess what I have learned is that it's pretty darn tough to be away from your wife and baby son for three years. I really feel that. And I guess of all the things of the war that bother me, that was the worst. That was very, very difficult. But like everybody else, you do what is asked of you for your country and for your family. And I feel it's worth it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So where was your first stop when you went overseas?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: New Guinea. Four degrees off the equator. And it was a pretty desolate, huge island. and they didn't have any welcome station for us or anything like that. As a matter of fact, I went over as what's called a casual; I was not attached to a unit. I was going over as a replacement or to enlarge the army. and I had 50 men to look after, a platoon. I never knew any of them until we got a troop train together and I was handed a list in a troop train, in a car full of men. But we got overseas and we were supposed to go to a replacement depot. So they went up coast a little ways and stopped the ship and we got -- had to go and climb down a cargo net and go into the ducks and we went ashore. And they took us in shore and dumped us off and left. The replacement depot wasn't there. So -- I don't know. I spent the war, I think, doing more looking after our own men than I did anything else. I felt responsible for them. We had to get water, so I had them dig a well with trenching shovels. And we needed food, and we had no communications, no transportation. So we were actually in a company of four platoons. We would send out -- we didn't have any weapons. Just the officers were armed. So we would send out a patrol with one weapon and three or four men to see if they could establish something or another. And they finally found a unit, and they started giving us food and communications and transportation, which was good because in about a month, I guess, or less -- two, three weeks, I guess -- I came down with a terrible situation. I remember very little of it, but I had dengue fever. And most people don't know anything about dengue fever. It's a tropical disease carried by mosquitos, and it's very painful. Every muscle and every joint in your body just aches and your fever gets very, very high. And I remember being carted off in the ambulance. I went to a field hospital -- a station hospital, actually. You have seen M.A.S.H.? I was in the unit which was about like M.A.S.H. And even today, I enjoy watching M.A.S.H. because that was really what much of my war was like. Not some of the -- we didn't have any women around. We didn't -- the officers up above us weren't as dumb as they portray in M.A.S.H. But the general situations and the mental processes and the disappointments that they have to go through at M.A.S.H. and the craziness of it, the funny things that happen. But I was in the hospital for two weeks sitting on the edge of the bunk waiting for the medical officer to say I could go back to the unit. He and another officer came through and he looked and he says, "Hey, Jack, come over here a minute and look at this. Is that it?" I said, "Come on, guys. Is that what?" Jack says, "Yeah, that's it." I says, "What's what?" He said, "You've got measles. We got to put you in quarantine." So I spent another week there. And finally got back to the unit. And I was eventually assigned to other units up the line and I moved away -- lost my troops and went up to actually do some ordnance work. And there were a lot of trials and tribulations, because I remember we weren't -- New Guinea is a place -- first of all, there's no roads, there's no electricity, there's no running water, there's no -- nothing. Once in while we would see one of the "fuzzy-wuzzies," the Papuans, but we were told to stay at least 100 feet away because most of them had malaria. If a mosquito would bite one of them and then bite us, then we'd get malaria. So we got up to a unit, finally. 207th Ordnance Maintenance Company, antiaircraft. Their specialty was maintaining the antiaircraft cannons and all of the weapons. First thing I did, they came out with Atabrine. Did you ever hear of Atabrine? It's a pill about the size of aspirin, but it's yellow. Bright, strong yellow color. What happened was when the Japanese took over the East Indies, they had sewed up the entire supply of the usual stuff that's -- I'm trying to think of the name of it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: It's not quinine?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Quinine. That's it. Thank you. They had all the quinine and we didn't have any to suppress the malaria. We started off, first day we had to take six of those aspirin-like yellow pills, and then one a day, every day. And they were right in the chow line. And as mess officer, I had to make sure that every man got his Atabrine pill every day. What's bad about that is that it does that by providing all of the symptoms of turning yellow. Your fingernails turn yellow, your eyeballs turn yellow, and your skin turns yellow. And your blood turns yellow. if you cut yourself, you don't get red blood anymore. Everything was yellow, just as though you had -- you would think somebody would have hepatitis. of course, it reacted the same way. It was working through the liver and that's why it got that yellow color. And incidentally, we stopped taking Atabrine -- the last five months of my service was up in occupied Japan, and we didn't need the Atabrine. So we took -- they stopped when we went up there. And I got home, I guess, about -- sometime in May of '46. But I was still tinged with yellow. It took a long time to dissolve out. So things were pretty good. But as I said, New Guinea, there was nothing to it. If we had any roads, it was because the engineers came through and cut them. And usually we worked along the north coast, and much of it was actually along the coast itself, because New Guinea is very, very mountainous. One of the bases that we were at, a place with a lot of other troops, it was kind of a staging area and we were working on all the weapons, getting them ready to check the units through, to make sure their weapons worked right. That was our job. But it was a half mile wide and about 25 miles long, all along the coast. And there was one road that ran the full length of it. So it was that kind of thing. And it was quite remote. We did have a company generator so that we could have electricity, but we had to shut it off -- shut the lights off at dark, at night anyway. And of course, being near the equator -- many people don't realize that the closer you get to the equator, the closer you get to a 12-hour, 12-hour day, 12 hours of daylight and 12 hours of night. Summer and winter, they're just about the same. And also, we were -- well, you have been in Painesville, you realize we have the sun coming up in the east and setting out in the lake. But where we were, the sun rose out of the ocean and set over back of the mountains. So we actually got darkness about 5:00 o'clock in the afternoon. And we made several other moves going up the line. Every time there was further need for us, we'd have to go. We shifted -- we shifted below -- between the Sixth Army and Eighth Army. And I am one of those who have great respect for General MacArthur. He's my hero, because I was there; I realized what he was up against. I know of all -- probably all of the latrine rumors that ever came around about the things that he was doing. But I thought, well, if he's got that much pleasures -- pleasures and privileges, fine. He's doing such a great job, he deserves them.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: I don't remember those rumors. Do you want to share any of those?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Well, they always come about. You know, about, "Well, you know, MacArthur isn't here; he's back in Australia." And I am intelligent enough to know, I guess, that that's where he had to be at that particular time. It was foolish for him to be up here. Although later we learned that he actually did come around. And it may not have been right during the middle of a gunfight, but I couldn't blame him for that. I wouldn't want him to be around. There were a lot of things, you know -- that type of thing. But he was a brilliant man. And I followed his career the rest of his life, actually. I know -- that's something else again.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Did you get a chance to meet him?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: I saw him once. It was a real thrill. But I was in the -- goofing off in downtown Tokyo and his headquarters were in the Dai Ichi Building. That's the No. 1 building in Tokyo. The Dai Ichi Building was his headquarters. And I saw him get out of his car and walk up the steps and salute his honor guard and go inside. that was thrilling. That was great.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So you were stationed down in New Guinea the whole time before you went to occupied Japan?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: No, no. No, no, no. What we were doing was preparing all these -- checking all the ordnance equipment, getting everybody supplied so they could invade the Philippines. When that started, of course, they needed us, so we went up into the Philippines. And I was in a different unit then. The number was the 307th instead of the 207th. But they switched us all around as the need -- if they needed a certain specialty, someone who was a specialist of something they would move them from one outfit to another. So I would have about five different addresses during the overseas time. We went and came in at Linguine Gulf, and that was quite -- that was quite an interesting situation, because all I can say is most of the area was cleared, and I'll let it go at that. I don't talk about those happenings. They get kind of mushy. And anyway, there were a lot of funny things.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You're welcome to talk about them. This is for the Library of Congress.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Okay. Well, most people watch the T.V. movies and all and think, "Boy, oh boy. Look at all those American tanks," and they read about General Patton. and he was a great man, too. But New Guinea was a place -- tanks wouldn't have done any good. First of all, you -- it had to be artillery and infantry that were doing the job. And most of the -- a lot of the artillery came from battleships. So I -- Finally, when I got into Luzon, up in the Linguine Gulf area, one of the jobs that I had, was assigned to do, was somebody had brought a tank ashore and they left it on the beach. So I had to get down to the beachhead, and I took two, three men with me that knew something about tanks, because I didn't. I had been -- in my OCS, we were taught how to drive a tank and I was licensed to drive a tank, but I didn't know anything about -- other than starting them and shifting gears, because the early M25 tank you had to shift gears in it, just to -- clutch and gears. And that was pretty big -- pretty bad. So anyway, I went down to the beach and we fired up the tank, and I remember we had to get gasoline for it, and stuff like that. So anyway, we went down and the first little town, San Fabian, and we were greatly thrilled because I was the tank commander up in the top and the men were down below and they had the ports open. But as we went down there, little kids came out in the street and they were all waving American flags. And we drove it over to the marshalling yard, and it was the only tank there. The rest were vehicles of all kinds, but -- so I saw that tank, and I saw two Japanese tankettes. They were the little two-man things. And I don't know why the Japs had them, because it just wasn't tank country. Luzon didn't have much, where -- we were up in the barrios. That's the boondocks. There wasn't much up there. Roads -- and of course, New Guinea, as I say, had no roads. And I remember distinctly, another fellow and I were driving down the road in a Jeep and I said, "Joe, something's wrong here. I don't know. I have got a gut feeling that something is -- I don't recognize, and I'm worried." He stopped the Jeep and he says, "Get out." And I got out and my feet were on a piece of concrete road. I hadn't ridden on a concrete road for so long, all during the training and coming over, and it was always a dirt road or gravel at best. But here was this concrete road. So we got out and did a little dance on it. So it's strange how you can miss things like that and not realize that you're doing without them all the time, and then you come back to reality. But it was fun. And part of us -- I don't know. We had different jobs to do. Some went up the coast up north, up towards the north end of the island. Lawan was the name of the town. And some went down towards Manila. and so I went over towards Balati Pass (ph). And that's enough of that. But I'd like -- oh, I'll tell you something about the Philippines that a lot of people don't understand. At least, there are -- First of all, it's a bunch of islands. Some of them are very small. Some of them, like Luzon, are a couple hundred miles long and a hundred miles wide. But the people that are there live in city or villages, barrios. A barrio is about like a county, actually. But each barrio has its own language. And they are as different as -- well, I came from around here, so I could understand a little bit of Finnish and Italian and Hungarian and Polish. These languages were as different as those. When we would go from one barrio from the next, if we wanted information from the people, we'd have to get an interpreter or talk to the kids. Now, the kids had gone to an American school, but the older people hadn't. So the kids spoke English as well as their own little language. And each language had a name. We were in Pongosi Nan (ph). Laudian (ph). Balati. Each one had a different language. But I did have the opportunity to talk to a school teacher in Bon Golden (ph); that was in the Pongosi Nan. And he showed me a textbook of history. and in that book -- I'm sorry -- yeah. It was history. And every place that the words "United States" or "America" appeared in that book, they had taken a razor blade and cut those words out. And they were really angered at the United States, and they were trying to teach that in school. They didn't want the kids to know how wonderful and great we were, but the kids knew. They understood. I did want to mention while I'm on the schooling that because there are some 120 different dialects or languages in the Philippines, when the Philippine soldiers -- when the army came in, they wanted to have schools, and they wanted all the kids to learn Japanese. So they were faced with a little problem: How do you take 120 different dialects and teach Japanese? They'd have to have how many different teachers? It would be a tremendous job. So they solved it by when they had schools, the kids would take one hour of English every day, and then two hours from English to Japanese. So that was their penalty for trying to get them to learn a strange language. But the little kids liked to speak English.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: So they were teaching them English.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: And they were great on that. And one of the things that really cheered me, and I remember the little -- some of the little kids had new pencils. And on the side was printed "I shall return. Douglas MacArthur." And they all wanted to be Americans. They wanted to come over here or at least, you know, have the American people there. So eventually, we -- I remember we went down south of Manila, to Batangus area. And we were being shipped out of there to go up into the occupation. And it was a very, very -- it was typical military foul-up, you know. We went down to the assigned area, and our particular company, we had 120 men, we had about 20 trucks, shop trucks of different kinds, and a wrecker and things like that. And the area they assigned us, I don't know who picked it out, but when the trucks went into the area and they were parked, and they just settled down right to the axles. It must have been an abandoned rice paddy or something. But it was a terrible thing. So we realized if we were going to move out when we had to, which would be in a day or two, we had to have some way out. And so my buddy and I went over and found the engineers and they brought a road grader over. And by gosh, they scraped a road for us and got us out of there. Otherwise, we'd still have been stuck there. Going into Japan was kind of a difficult thing, because we had no love for the Japanese people at all. They were just -- well, I shouldn't mention -- I don't know. I guess I can mention the fact that -- I feel it was a latrine rumor. You know, a latrine rumor? They -- the latrine rumor said if we would bring in a Japanese prisoner live, we could have a case of beer and a weekend in Manila when it opened up. And it was that kind of stuff. I don't know. We were support troops. We weren't really sent to eliminate the Japanese ourselves; we would help the guys that were doing it. But it was that kind of a situation. And you develop a hatred. And of course, I felt it very much, because I rationalized that they were the people that were keeping me away from my wife and my little boy. So I really didn't care much for them. However, we had to go up in the occupation. and I can remember we were on an LST and going in and docking, and I was carrying my carbine. And I thought I would be smart to unload that thing, because the initial sight of Japanese men and -- walking around. But I guess I finally realized, you know, hey, the war is over. It's time to get this show on the road here and get home. So I entered into the spirit of the thing and put my carbine up on the shelf and did what I had to do. I had a very interesting job. In Tokyo, I was assigned to build a tire depot. And I had -- I just had about 10 men, about one squad from our company, but we had about 35 Japanese men employed. And they gave us as the spot, an empty plot of ground and a five-story bombed-out building. That was the Victor Record Company. Remember Victrolas? The Victor Record Company was right there and had about probably three acres of ground with it. It was right on the canal. And the operation was that the tires would be shipped from the United States and come over and unloaded from a freighter onto a barge. And the barge would come up the canal, and then they were unloaded and we would store them. So we -- I said, "Well, fine. What size tires are you getting?" And he said, "All kinds." And we ended up storing everything. Well, the first job was -- I didn't want to put them right on the bare ground. So I got -- I wanted some dunnage. And one of the corporals that I had, and I don't know where he got the information, he says, "I can get you some wood platforms. How would you like that?" I says, "Where do you get platforms?" He says, "Well, where I was before, where they took me from, we were getting Jeeps and three-quarter tons and the two-and-a-half ton six-bys from the States, and they were shipped boxed. They had the wheels taken off and the top and everything, and they came in a crate." And he said, "Those crates are just sitting up there." So I got him a truck in a couple of minutes and said, "Go get them." And they spent about a week bringing those box sides. They would get every one of them -- the top and bottom and the four sides -- and bring them back and we put them on the ground as dunnage underneath the stacks of tires. We were getting anything -- wheelbarrow tires, airplane tires, Piper Cub tires, and Jeep and truck and recon -- all sizes of tires. And even road grader tires. These were these massive things. You have seen the great big size of them. And I was a little worried, because when we got them out -- well, the first four or five wasn't bad, but when we would get them up -- we had to pile them up over our heads, pyramid style. And they would get about 12 of those little Japanese -- and the Japanese people are small. Most of them are midgets compared to -- I was a little guy in the army, but they were all smaller than I was. But You get around 12 to 14 lifting one of those things and moving it and putting it up there. And I said, "Hey, if somebody slips, we're going to have a lot of mashed Japs here." But we got the tire depot done and it was very nice. Funny little incidents happened. The Japanese, the workers from the Victor Record Company, they were trying to start up. And they had a Japanese naval officer who was managing the thing. And I talked to him one time, and I said, "Where did you learn this perfect English?" I said, "You have no trouble at all." He said, "I'm a graduate of U.C.L.A." And so I asked him about what he did in the war, and he said he served in the navy, and he's a naval officer, and he's a civilian now, and he's running Victor Records. So the workers that lived there would come around and they'd build a fire and heat water for tea. When lunchtime came, they would all -- I don't know where they carried them, but they would suddenly appear with a little lunch box and pair of chopsticks, and they would be eating and having tea. There was a little girl there, a young girl, and I noticed she had a bad cut on her hand. And, you know, I feel -- it's something I could do. So the next day I brought her a bandaid, and so I showed her how to wash it up and put the bandaid on. And, oh, she was very thankful. Three days later, she brought me a nice little box with a Japanese doll in it. I didn't want to take it, because I know it was a family heirloom. This is what these people have. But she insisted that I take it. I mailed it home to Jeannette. And Jeannette still doesn't like the Japanese. She's very bitter about those three years, and I don't blame her. I tried to get along. I tried to learn a little of their language. I went to night school to learn a little Japanese. And of course, I had to learn some of the markings anyway, because they were -- Our primary job then, we went up to Tokyo and we operated the Tokyo ordnance depot. And the Japanese had to turn in all of the swords that they had -- family swords, military swords, any kind of a sword at all, whether it was a ceremonial sword or family heirloom. And we had -- unfortunately, there was no way we could keep track of what kind of came in, the trainloads, boxcar loads. And we would have to store the stuff. That was the rule. So -- and they sent their weapons to us. And they -- we even had one motorcycle, army -- Japan army motorcycle. The guys fixed it up and they rode it all around the place. It was a very big depot. I think there were 21 big concrete two-story buildings, so we had a lot of room. And we used a lot of Japanese laborers, too. We hired Japanese laborers for everything. One of the problems we found out, of course, water is not purified the way it is here in the pipes. So, you know, the drinking water or anything like that, we still had to get our drinking water out of the lister bags that we could get filled from the engineering, the engineers' water points. We wanted some KPs, kitchen police, Japanese, so we could not have to put any of our own men on that duty. So I contacted the labor boss; that was a woman. Well, she was a real hard worker, very hard-nosed and tough about the whole thing. But she ran -- she could get us laborers. Well, I told her I needed -- I could use up to eight. She said, "How about six." "Well, six and we'll work them hard, extra hard, that's all." But she lined -- had ten of them and she said, "Well, first, they have to go over to the medics and get checked out." And there were two of them that were -- two of them were disqualified because they had TB; their TB patch came out and they wouldn't take them. And four of them, I remember they wouldn't take them because they had worms. So she lined up another ten, and we checked them. She finally gave us eight KPs, and they were all healthy guys. So one of them, Joe Yumagachi, Joe spoke perfect English. I said, "What happened, Joe?" He said, "I was born in Chicago. And when I was 10, my father and mother brought me back to Japan. And I had to go to school here" and -- But he said -- he knows America, and he said he was -- he felt bad about -- you know, he knew that -- what was going on, and he felt very bad about it, but he said he had to keep his mouth shut. And he was a great boy. I really appreciated having him. He helped me out a lot, because he would act as an interpreter when I got stuck. And he asked for a favor one time. I said, "Okay, Joe. What is it that you want? If I can do it, I'll do it." He said he wanted a pass to go across the island of Honshu. He had some relatives over on the China Seas coast, over on the other side. And I said, "Well, what do you mean?" "Well," he says, "you know," he says, "we can't travel without a pass." So I told the company clerk, I says, "Take one of our -- use the company letterhead and write out a pass that he's permitted to go to this city," and I signed it. And Joe got his weekend travel, he could travel over there. They don't have -- they didn't have very many vehicles, but their trains were still running and they did have good passenger service on the trains. And I was always amazed because every Japanese understood the word "station." And I know what happened, of course. Our engineers went over and helped them or they came over here and learned about a train station. So you could always -- if you wanted to identify where you were at -- in other words, we were near Akabani Station. And people would know where Akabani Station is. It's like when you say Wycliffe Station or Painesville Depot or something like that. It was a great time. I don't know. I finally -- I finally worked out of it. I got rid of the hatred, I guess, because I saw that those people did not have -- they did not have the room. Their population was big, and Honshu was just like New Guinea; it was a little bit of shoreline and then there were mountains. And it was very, very crowded for them. So I could understand why they would want to enlarge the physical area of their country. It's no excuse. I don't think it was the right thing to do, but I could understand how they would get to that point. But I can remember driving down the street in the Jeep, and their streets were very narrow. And of course, their houses are wood and paper. Paper instead of glass. And we had to follow the honey wagon. And I had the opportunity -- I tried to get to know the people and get invited to their homes, you know, so I could see just what are they really like. and so I did. And I found out that their bathroom conditions were -- the bathrooms are nice and clean, but the actual sewage problem is something else again. Their -- instead of having a regular toilet seat and lid, there was a board, probably about 8 inches wide and 2 feet long and rounded on the ends. And it had a handle to it, and you could lift it up and there was a hole in the floor. And underneath that was a bucket, wooden bucket. (END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE.) (BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE.) MR. JOHNSON: Well, I was saying that I was in a Jeep following a honey wagon, and it was loaded with barrels. It was a flatbed trailer, horsedrawn. And the fellow would stop at each house and he'd take a clean bucket or two and go, and bring back a covered bucket. But, whoa. I didn't know what I was doing there, but I got off that road just as quickly as I could. But -- so much of their country was like that. and I remember the first time that I went from Yokohama to Tokyo. That was about 25 miles, right along the coast. And that was the area that was firebombed. And it really tore at my gut to see that. If you can picture miles and miles with a two-lane road down the middle of it, but off to each side hundreds -- you know, five, six hundred feet on either side, and there was about a foot of wood ashes. Just white ash was all that was there. And then in most of the places you could see standing up there would be a small iron safe. Rusted, of course. But the safe was the only thing that was left. And everything else was just burnt up. But, you know, that's what it took. And it's one of the -- but it kind of impinges on people. And you realize that Sherman was right. And I guess I get -- I don't know, a little -- feel too much for people. And I can remember one of the families that lived nearby, and the fellow worked for us and he had a little baby. And so I was going to be real nice and helpful, and so I swiped a can of milk from our supplies in the kitchen and I took over a can of milk for them, because they had no milk in Japan that was -- I found out. As a matter of fact, they don't even have a word for table milk as we know it, it's so rare. I had a hard time explaining what it was. I thought she would like the milk to wean the baby, you know, when the time came. But I had a very difficult time. I didn't know how to explain it. I didn't know the Japanese word that would correspond to it. I don't know whether there is one or not. But that was kind of the way I went through the war, I guess. I hated to see the destruction. I hated to see -- any of the bad things, I tried to ignore them. I know that they're there, but I don't dwell on them. I don't like to talk about them. I don't like to see them. I never watch -- I shouldn't say -- I seldom watch a war movie on T.V. I did see a little of -- last night, there was a remake of All Quiet on the Western Front. But I had seen the earlier picture years I read the book, so I knew what it was, and so I wanted to see what they were doing moviewise. But anyway, I finally came back. And I remember -- I remember the trip back and we were supposed to -- we came back on a big troop transport, the Marine Raider. It was a fast -- it carried about 5,000 troops. And we were all set and we had to stay about three days just before we could load. And finally got there. And generally on the troop ships, like anyplace else, the officers are quartered up on A deck and then the sergeants on the first, and then men down below in the holds. Well, it seemed that when we got on board we found out that there were a lot of merchant seamen who were deadheading back to the States. But they belonged to the union, and they said, "We have to be quartered in the A deck. None of this stuff in the holds for us." So we were put down in the fifth level down. and you were assigned a cot and a place to hang up your gear, and that was about it. Well, I'm not much on -- I don't enjoy being 20, 30 feet under water anyway. So there was another lieutenant there that wanted to be -- he felt the same way I did. So we took our blankets and we slept on deck. We went up onto A deck and took our blankets and slept there all the way back. And I remember getting home and I came -- I was discharged from the -- separated from Camp Atterbury, Indiana, and given a train ticket to Cleveland. So I got into the terminal tower, and I went to the soldiers' and sailors' relief counter. And I explained the situation: I was coming back out of the army after three years away from my wife and boy, and we lived in the family farmhouse over here across the street. And I thought, well, it's going to be kind of tough. I would like to spend a day or two in a hotel in Cleveland with my wife, getting acquainted again. So they were very nice. They got a hotel room for us and had her drive into Cleveland and we reunited after three years. Of course, we had seen each other a little bit. At the end of the first year, I got 15 days leave right after commissioning. Then I had to report back to Aberdeen. But it was a long time. But, you know, my wife and I each wrote a letter every day that we could. And I suppose I managed about an average of five days a week, and she wrote every day. Now, this is back -- you have seen mail call? We had mail call every day, and I didn't get any mail and I didn't get any mail and I didn't get any mail. Sixty days -- I got sixty letters. And all the time I was writing, and I never knew whether my mail was getting home. I had no -- there was no telephone, no way -- I was just completely lost. I might as well have been at the North Pole. And that impinged. So -- and we were only allowed to write we were -- on the letter we could write "Somewhere in New Guinea." That was -- we weren't allowed to mention anything about it other than that. So I had a great time. And the mail would eventually catch up with us like that. But I thought, 60 days, they got to be kidding. And I wondered if my mail was that late getting back. And, of course, some of the letters never got through, either. MR. SWOPE: What kinds of things did she write to you?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: What kind of things would she write in letters to you?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Well, she would tell me about how Curt, our son, was doing, his latest antics, and if she had been able to take him someplace and how he behaved. And I remember one time she said, "He was a real pest today. He laid down on the floor of the store and just hollered and cried." And she finally had to take him out and take him away. Things like that. Things of interest. And once in a while, my dad would come over and he'd get hold of some film and he'd take some photos and send them to me. I kept all the letters. I still have them, and she has mine. I guess that's why -- last June, we celebrated 60 years. And it's been that kind of a marriage, I guess.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Were you able to write much at all to her, or did it have to be very general stuff?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: I tried to be as honest as I could, you know. And I got into trouble once that way one time. I used to write as much as I could, but I couldn't do too much. You know, but I could describe the area we were in. We were on the coast at one time and there was a beautiful sand beach, and there were coconuts around. and couple of the guys made the mistake of trying to climb up the palm tree and getting coconuts. And he got up there and found out that the place was also inhabited by an army of ants and a great big crab, and he came down a lot faster than he went up. And in order to get up, what he did, he borrowed two of our pistol belts and hooked them together and used that as a climbing device to get up the palm tree. And he was good at it. And he took some skin off the inside of his arms and legs, too. But he did knock down some coconuts. And the men -- we finally had to put a stop to it, but they were -- one fellow would take his bayonet in his hand and the other would stand about 10 or 12 feet away and he would toss up a coconut in the air and -- a green coconut now -- and the other fellow would try to impale it on his bayonet. But it got to be too close, because some of them -- those coconuts were a little tougher than what they looked like, and the first thing you know, the bayonet would be pointed back towards us. So no more. Another time we were right on the edge of the ocean on a coral ledge, and that was wonderful because we were able to -- we had a little wooden dock. Not a dock, but just a place where we could dive into the ocean. And it was about -- I don't know, 25, 30 feet deep. You could look down in the bottom and there was nothing. Just beautiful coral and South Pacific ocean. Just the kind of things you see in the movies. It was wonderful. And one day there our warrant officer was a little bit bored. So he took six blocks of nitro starch, an explosive, and put a blasting cap and a fuse and lit the fuse and threw it into the ocean. And there was a nice big whump and a big spray of water. Well, after the -- I won't say dust, but after the ocean cleared, we could see a couple of great big long fish down there, laying on their side. Anyway, just shortening the story, I of course got to show off. And I dove down and grabbed one of them by the tail and brought it up. And it was pretty good-sized. Nineteen pounds. And there was another one down there, so I went down. And I'm not a trained diver at all, but I learned how to swim and I learned how to surface dive and I used to swim underwater a lot at the old YMCA. but I had never been down that deep before, but I went down and got the other one and brought it up. That was 23 pounds. So I had the cook dress those fish out and cook them for supper. Every man that wanted a fillet of fish, he get a little square of fish, if you wanted fresh meat. And that was a wonderful thing, to have something like that. For the ones that liked it. Some, of course, don't eat fish. But that's all right, too. So those are the kind of things that I would write. I tried to stay away -- oh, I did -- I told you I got into a little trouble. I met a fellow from Painesville, Kenny Winkle. And Kenny was about four or five, six years older than I was. Oh, more than that, I guess. But I had known him since I was, oh, 8 years old. I don't remember when I met Kenny. At a YMCA camp. And he was in the engineers, and when I went to the engineers one time for some help, I heard this voice that said, "That looks like someone from Painesville." And that was Ken. And he said, "You know, Bob Radcliff is here, too. He's with the engineers over at the air strip, about four or five miles away." And I said, "Geez, we ought to see if we can't get together. Can you get hold of him?" He says, "Yeah, I'll set it up. I'll give you a call." So we had an old military phone there, and Kenny finally got through to me. So I took the company Jeep and picked up Ken and we went over to Bob Radcliff's and spent an evening. That was a wonderful time. We had a half a bottle of booze to kill, which was something else. But we just enjoyed it. Bob had a nice place. He had a parametal tent for quarters. And what he had done was to take a parachute and put that up inside the tent so he had white silk walls. And it was -- people would do that just to, hey, this is great. We had a wonderful time. So I wrote that to Jeannette. And the next day I got a letter off and told her about the wonderful time I had with Kenny Winkle, my old friend, and Bob Radcliff who was in my class at Harvey High School. And of course, it took a little while for that letter to get home. And the day it -- And I told her, "You know, I just want to show you, don't worry about us. We're in real good shape. we have a lot of fun. We are enjoying this. I miss you. I wish you were here, or I wish I were home. But everything is fine here. Don't panic. Don't worry." That letter arrived the same day that in the Painesville Telegraph they published the death of Ken Winkle. He had been moving up with his engineering troops and he was killed. So I heard about that. But I remember sending a nice letter. Not nice -- but I sent a letter of regret to his wife, because -- they had no children, but I knew both Ken and his wife, and I thought that was the least I could do is say that at the time we met him we had a wonderful time and he was in good shape and all. So that's about the size of the --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: Do you remember hearing the news when they dropped the bomb?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Oh, yes. Yes, I do. I do. We were on Luzon. And I remember, I had -- I was -- had some of my men together, and one of them says, "So what's -- they make a bomb out of an atom; that must be kind of small." I says, "Well, I don't know exactly how they do it. This is somewhat new. But I do remember in high school chemistry, our chemistry teacher -- well, it was written right in the chemistry book, so I'm sure it's pretty well -- there's enough energy in a pound of coal to drive a 100-car freight train 21 times around the earth, if you can unlock that power." I said, "I think that's what they have done. I don't know how they did it or where, but I suppose it has something like the radioactivity of radium or something of that nature. But I really don't know. But I'm like you. I've got to find out." And of course when we got the word, we were very, very happy. We realized -- I guess it just kind of stultified everybody; we just couldn't believe it. it was somehow strange. You know, no more did we have to worry about anything. And -- great. So we were very pleased and we realized -- because we knew that, you know, if we had had to go up there, hey, once more was just once more; that's all. And we weren't too happy about the thought of going into Japan. And after I got there and had a chance to see what they had -- because I did see some of their stores. One of my men came in one day and said, "Do you want to go up -- take us up the mountain and I'll show you where a Jap cave is up there." So we went up and I hated to go in the thing, because it was just a very tiny entrance into the side of the mountain and the passageway was very narrow. I had to turn sideways to inch down in there sideways. and we came into a room and it was full of Japanese radios, military. So I thought well, boy, they really got things -- you know, if somebody wants to try to lay them down anywhere on this island, it's going to be pretty rough because they have got stores hidden away, you can never destroy them. And so that was it.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You didn't tour Hiroshima or Nagasaki or --

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: I did not. But I had some of my friends who were down there. And they said it's very similar to what we saw in -- between Yokohama and Tokyo area. It's quite a bit like that. Everything is -- most of the things were destroyed. I did learn one interesting thing in Japan, going to visit a fellow who had been in Japan. He lived up on the mountainside, heading up on the hillside. He had a very nice house, but he had been employed by -- I don't know whether it was -- one of the British companies, and they just kept him right there. He was -- for some reason or other, they didn't imprison him or anything. I think they wanted to use him after the war to establish commerce with Britain. But as I was going up there, I noticed there had been some bomb damage, bombs go off, and there was a concrete wall which had some breaks in it. And I had a chance to look at them close, and it suddenly struck me these Japanese are very, very smart people in a way, because they realized that a concrete wall -- and this was poured concrete. It wasn't block; it was poured -- but it would need some kind of reinforcement. We used rebar and mesh and this and that and the other thing, and chains and old pipe for reinforcing; they didn't have that. But they did use strips about an inch wide or half inch to an inch wide, long strips of bamboo. And I don't know if you have worked much with bamboo, but it will cut crosswise with a saw and it will split lengthwise with a knife. But it's very strong. it has a great tensile strength to it. And that's what they were using in their concrete walls. So I have to give them credit for something.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: When you think of that experience overseas, does anything come to mind as the most vivid memory of that?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: I don't -- I really haven't thought about that much. I don't think there's any one thing that, you know, stands out.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: No particular incident or anything like that? That doesn't come to mind?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: No. Not really. Just the overall picture, of course. We were without so much. We missed so much. And one thing that bothered me, of course, it really surprised me going a very, very long period of time -- I mean, I'm talking about months, years even, seemed like a couple years -- without hearing a woman's voice. Somehow I missed that, I guess, because, you know, family and going to school and this and that, you always hear girls' voices and to not hear one -- everything is a man's voice. And it's startling then the first time you hear a woman's voice. There were women on -- you remember the WACS? There were WACS on New Guinea. And I saw one time their compound. But you could always tell where the WACS were, because where they worked and where they lived and everything about them, there was a big barbed-wire fence and an armed guard walking on the perimeter. He wasn't allowed inside. He walked outside that -- and that's the way they shielded them. But we knew it was the WACS' compound. But you don't realize things like that. I guess just like I told you about the street, going without a street. And I try to remember the funny things. I don't like to talk too much -- well, I shouldn't -- well, I'll tell you one funny -- to me, I laugh at it. I really think it deserves mentioning. On Luzon, we were in a rice paddy area so there was a lot of open sky. And there was an air raid one night. And the signal for an air raid, of course, one of the antiaircraft cannon would fire three rounds up in the air -- bam, bam, bam -- and then, hey, you -- and it was a very clear night. Moonlight night. And so it was kind of quiet, and I was just standing around with a couple of other guys and all of a sudden there was a Japanese Betty Bomber, and I don't know why, but he was flying just about treetop level, coming over us. And before anybody could do anything, he was gone. But one of the guys hollered and said, "Hey, that guy was smoking a Camel cigarette!" So right in the midst of a very tense situation, our guys still could make jokes: "Relax, you know. It's okay." So it's all right. But a few things like that. Well, I think I have --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: You think you have covered it?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Covered it pretty well.

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: This is the most extensive I have heard about the Japanese occupation. I've talked to a couple other guys who were involved in that, but you have given me a lot of insight into that.

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Well, I'm glad I got to do it, because I think it really educated me, gave me an appreciation for what we had done. And also I respect the people that were the cause of all this, because they had --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: One guy told me that at first the Japanese people kept their distance from the soldiers that were over there, and then slowly they started -- did that happen with you?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: I don't think so. We didn't mix too well, but I never found too much difficulty. Once I learned a few words of Japanese and when our work brought us together, I didn't experience any animosity. I mean, they were -- I think they didn't know whether to apologize or just what, and whether they -- you know, they knew they had done something wrong, but they didn't want to have it held against them. I felt --

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: They were humbled by it?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Yes, very. But -- I can remember one scene that -- one of their -- we did have workers, as I say. And one of them, they found out had swiped a roll of toilet paper. I couldn't blame him because, you know, there were no stores; there was nothing like that around there. And a roll of toilet paper, I thought, well, if he wants that for his house, he's probably got a wife and children at home and he's trying to get something for them. You know, the foreman called the men together, and he had the fellow bow down in front of him, which they do in recognition, and he made him take the roll of toilet paper out from under his jacket and hand it to him. And the fellow handed it over, and the boss handed it over to one of the others. And all of a sudden, just out of -- this guy, he came and he hit that guy right across the face a terrible blow, and the fellow just stood there and bowed. And he came the other way and slapped his face. And I thought, "Geez. That guy's hurting." And so I could hear him telling them, and I figured -- he said, you know, "If you ever do anything like that again," and I think he said something about you could come back in a week -- "And if you ever do anything like that again, we'll have every man in this unit -- or this group will give you the slapping that I did."

sp.speaker: Thomas Swope
sp.p: The foreman was Japanese, too?

sp.speaker: Edward T. Johnson
sp.p: Yeah. They were all Japanese watching them. They were all Japanese entirely. But he really let the guy know that you just don't swipe off the American army.
[END OF INTERVIEW]
